title: What a Leader Does With Anger
subtitle: How a pastor tells righteous anger from unrighteous anger, why most ministry anger is wounded pride wearing the mask of zeal, and the slow work of letting God redeem a leader's temper.

sections.title: The Question Is Not Whether You Feel It
sections.body:
Anger is going to come. It is not optional for a leader who cares about anything. You will feel it when the wolf comes for the sheep, when the gossip spreads, when the lazy man wastes what the faithful man built, when injustice walks into your church wearing a smile.

The question is never whether you will feel anger. The question is what you do with it once you do. Scripture does not tell us to never be angry. It tells us to be angry and sin not, which means there is a way to be angry that is holy and a way that is hell, and the difference between them is the whole battle.

Most leaders never ask the question. They simply feel the heat and act on it, and call whatever follows righteous because they were the one who felt it.

sections.title: Righteous Anger Is Anger at the Right Things
sections.body:
There is an anger that is the shadow of love. Jesus made a whip and drove the moneychangers out of the temple, not because His ego was bruised but because His Father's house had been turned into a market and the poor were being robbed in the name of God. He looked at hard hearts and was grieved and angry at once.

Righteous anger is provoked by what provokes God. It burns at sin, at injustice, at the harm done to the weak. It does not burn for itself. And here is the test that exposes almost all of ours. Righteous anger is slow to come, controlled in its expression, and aimed at the wrong, not the person. It seeks to set things right, not to make someone pay.

God is slow to anger. The leader whose anger is fast and frequent should suspect that very little of it is the holy kind.

sections.title: Most of My Anger Is Just My Pride With a Sunburn
sections.body:
Let me be honest about my own. The vast majority of my anger has not been zeal for God. It has been wounded pride, frustrated control, a plan interrupted, a name slighted, a comfort threatened. It dressed itself up in spiritual language, but underneath it was just the self, defending itself, furious that the world would not bend.

This is the anger James warns about, the anger of man that does not produce the righteousness of God. It feels righteous from the inside. That is its great deception. The angry man is always certain his cause is just, which is exactly why anger is such a poor judge of its own legitimacy.

Before you act on your anger, ask the humbling question. Am I angry for God, or am I just angry for me. The honest answer changes everything that comes next.

sections.title: Be Slow, and Do Not Let the Sun Go Down on It
sections.body:
The discipline of anger has two halves. The first is to be slow. Quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. The leader who builds a pause between the feeling and the action will sin far less, because most of the damage anger does is done in the first hot minute before the mind catches up.

The second half is not to let it sit. Do not let the sun go down on your anger, Paul says, because anger left overnight curdles into resentment, and resentment hardens into bitterness, and bitterness is a root that defiles a man and everyone near him. Deal with it the same day. Forgive, confront, repent, release, but do not file it away to feed on later.

Slow to start. Quick to settle. That is the rhythm of a leader who rules his temper instead of being ruled by it.

sections.title: God Can Redeem the Fire if You Let Him Hold It
sections.body:
The goal is not to become a man who feels nothing. A leader who has killed his capacity for anger has usually killed his capacity for love along with it, because the two run on the same current. The goal is a man whose fire is governed, aimed, and laid before God, so that the heat that once wounded the flock now defends it.

Moses had a temper that murdered a man in Egypt. The same temper, under God, became holy indignation against a stubborn nation, and even that he learned to carry to God instead of pouring on the people. God did not remove the fire. He redeemed it.

Bring your anger to Him. The temper that has cost you so much can become, in His hands, a strength that finally serves. But only if you let Him hold the fire, and stop trying to be the one who decides where it burns.
